```{r setup}
#| include: false
# Figures come from scripts/90_report_figs.R (figs/<figure>_<profile>.png + manifest.csv).
# The CONUS ("full") version of a figure is shown when it exists, otherwise the dev one.
figs <- if (file.exists("figs/manifest.csv")) {
  utils::read.csv("figs/manifest.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
} else data.frame(figure = character(), profile = character())

show_fig <- function(name, caption, alt = caption) {
  m <- figs[figs$figure == name, , drop = FALSE]
  pick <- intersect(c("full", "dev"), m$profile)
  pick <- pick[file.exists(sprintf("figs/%s_%s.png", name, pick))]
  if (!length(pick)) {
    cat(sprintf('\n::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}\n## Figure pending\n%s\n:::\n\n',
                caption))
    return(invisible())
  }
  r <- m[m$profile == pick[1], ][1, ]
  note <- sprintf("[%s · %s · figure made %s]{.fig-meta}", r$extent, r$years, r$made)
  cat(sprintf('\n![%s %s](figs/%s_%s.png){#fig-%s fig-alt="%s" .column-page-right}\n\n',
              caption, note, name, pick[1], gsub("_", "-", name), alt))
}
```

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## First results, October 2026 (preliminary)
The analysis and its checks have run; the results below are first numbers from 13–24 seasons per
region, shared for review with the project partners. It is a companion to the
[fuel phenology regions page](index.html) and the [NPN curing study](npn_study.html).
:::

## At a glance

**Main findings (preliminary).**

- **Dryness first.** Dead-fuel dryness from PRISM improves predictions of fire starts and fire
  growth in all six pilot regions; the NFDRS 1000-hour fuel moisture does better than a simple
  60-day water balance everywhere but California.
- **Curing adds to fire growth.** Weeks with more herbaceous fuel cured than usual have more fire
  in every region. Adding the satellite's weekly cured-fuel share improves held-out predictions of
  fire growth (2012–2024) in about three years of four, in all five regions tested, and of
  human-caused fire starts; not of lightning starts.
- **The signal is real.** It survives leaving out burned cells and adding this week's air dryness,
  and it beats 20 of 20 random reshufflings of the years.
- **It is the observed fuel state that counts.** Curing dates forecast two weeks ahead from
  weather add nothing; a cured share built from the 16-day satellite composites available each
  week does not carry the growth signal either. Monitoring would need faster data.
- **The GSI and the satellite carry different information.** The NFDRS2016 GSI's value for fire is
  mostly its vapour-pressure-deficit term, strongest in the monsoon Southwest; the satellite adds
  fuel-curing information the GSI lacks in California and the Great Plains.
- **C3/C4:** there is no gap between cool- and warm-season grass growth to produce a fire dip. On
  the ground (NPN sites with both types), warm-season grasses green up months before cool-season
  grasses cure, in every region and year checked; the satellite curves cannot separate the two.

**The question.** At the scale of a region and a season, does the green-up and curing of
grasses and other herbaceous plants shape fire activity? The regions work built typical
green-up and curing dates for every 4 km cell, and both its ground check and the NPN curing
study found that weather rules don't beat the typical date against single-plant ground
dates. Fire activity is a regional, fuel-bed-scale response, the scale fire managers care
about, and it is the one verification source with good coverage of herbaceous fuels in the
Southwest and California.

**Two tests.**

1. **Seasonal:** does each region's fire season open and close at green-up and curing, for
   example a spring window on last year's cured grass that closes at green-up, and a fall
   window that opens at curing?
2. **Year to year:** in years when curing or green-up runs early or late, does fire activity
   shift with it, once dead-fuel dryness and the number of ignitions are accounted for? The
   answer is how much the phenology improves predictions for years left out of the fit, not
   a correlation.

A third question comes from partners in the northern Plains: in mixed prairie, does fire
activity dip in the gap between the cool-season and warm-season growth pulses?

## Design

| Element | Choice |
|---|---|
| Fire starts | FPA-FOD 7th edition (1992–2024): wildfires reaching 10 acres or more, by discovery week, all causes; lightning and human separately for 2001–2019 |
| Fire growth | VIIRS active fire (S-NPP, 2012 onward; NOAA-20 fills S-NPP outage days): unique 375 m pixel-days |
| Burned area | FPA-FOD final fire size, by discovery date (all fires of 10 acres or more); MTBS perimeters (large fires, 2001–2023) show what fuel burned |
| Phenology | Yearly satellite green-up (NDVI 20 %) and curing (NDVI end of season, 50 %) dates for every 4 km cell, 2001–2025, and the typical-date maps |
| Dead-fuel baseline | Rainfall minus potential evaporation over the last 60 days (simple and readable), then the 1000-hour dead fuel moisture computed from PRISM (NFDRS 1978 equations) in its place; checks: Keetch–Byram drought index and 30-day mean vapour pressure deficit |
| Weather | PRISM daily 4 km only |
| Herbaceous cover | NLCD grassland, shrub/scrub, pasture/hay and herbaceous wetland share; in the upper Midwest and Great Plains, phenology from cells at least 35 % herbaceous |
| Unit | Region × week × year (weeks are fixed 7-day blocks from January 1), herbaceous cells |
| Model | One pooled count model with region effects; skill judged leaving one year out |
| Years | 2001–2024 for fire starts; 2012–2024 where starts and growth overlap |
| Pilot regions | Monsoon Southwest (3), interior West (6, 12), California annual grasslands (11), northern and central Great Plains (10), upper Midwest (13) |

: Study design {.striped}

The FPA-FOD record holds wildfires only: planned ignitions (prescribed fires) were left out
when the database was built, except prescribed fires that escaped and needed suppression
(Short 2014). Fire names that look like prescribed burns are counted by region as a check.
Agricultural and prescribed burning are screened out (fire records coded as debris or open
burning; satellite detections on cropland or not linked to a reported fire), and the share
each screen removes is reported by region. In the northern Plains and upper Midwest a
snow-off date from PRISM is part of the baseline, because spring fire there depends on
snowmelt as well as green-up.

## First look: fire records (October 17)

The FPA-FOD 7th edition holds 2.66 million records for 1992–2024. For 2001–2024 in the lower 48,
1.94 million fall on the analysis grid; 193,000 reached 10 acres or more and were not debris or
open burning, 52,900 of them in the six pilot regions. Fire names that look like prescribed
burns are negligible (under 20 per region).

| Region | Fires ≥ 10 ac | Lightning | Human | Unknown cause | Debris share of human fires ≥ 10 ac | On strict herbaceous cells |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3 Monsoon Southwest | 9,051 | 51 % | 43 % | 6 % | 13 % | 68 % |
| 6 Interior West | 9,603 | 57 % | 40 % | 3 % | 15 % | 71 % |
| 12 Interior West | 5,161 | 41 % | 54 % | 5 % | 15 % | 75 % |
| 11 California annual grasslands | 9,349 | 4 % | 68 % | 27 % | 6 % | 64 % |
| 10 Northern and central Great Plains | 12,355 | 40 % | 53 % | 7 % | 18 % | 70 % |
| 13 Upper Midwest | 7,405 | 4 % | 85 % | 12 % | 36 % | 5 % |

: Wildfires of 10 acres or more (debris and open burning removed), 2001–2024 {.striped}

**Seasonal shape.** The share of each region's fires by month already shows the windows the
study is about:

| Region | Jan | Feb | Mar | Apr | May | Jun | Jul | Aug | Sep | Oct | Nov | Dec |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | 2 | 5 | 7 | 10 | 13 | 23 | 20 | 11 | 3 | 3 | 2 | 2 |
| 6 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 13 | 36 | 31 | 10 | 3 | 1 | 0 |
| 12 | 0 | 0 | 2 | 2 | 6 | 20 | 35 | 22 | 9 | 3 | 1 | 0 |
| 11 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 2 | 11 | 22 | 24 | 17 | 11 | 7 | 2 | 1 |
| 10 | 1 | 2 | 6 | 6 | 3 | 8 | 29 | 26 | 11 | 5 | 3 | 1 |
| 13 | 1 | 2 | 13 | 36 | 16 | 2 | 5 | 5 | 5 | 9 | 5 | 1 |

: Percent of each region's fires of 10 acres or more by discovery month {.striped}

The upper Midwest (13) has a sharp spring peak (March–May, 65 %) that collapses in June, and a
smaller fall rise in October: the dormant-grass windows on either side of the growing season.
The Great Plains (10) shows a human-caused March–April window before green-up and a summer
lightning season. In the monsoon Southwest (3) human fires run February–June and lightning
fires peak in June–July, before the monsoon greens the grass.

**Data issues found.**

- *Reporting change from 2020.* Records switch from separate federal and non-federal sources
  to a single interagency source in 2020–2021. Yearly counts stay continuous, but the share
  with an unknown cause rises in every pilot region (to 10–30 %), and in California (11) to
  50–86 % in 2020–2024, mostly state and local records. Splitting lightning from human starts
  is reliable only to 2019 in California, and less reliable after 2019 elsewhere.
- *Fire locations in the upper Midwest.* Only 5 % of region 13's fires are on strict
  herbaceous cells; the typical fire cell is 1 % grassland and shrub, 14 % open herbaceous
  including pasture and hay, and 37 % cropland. Herbaceous fuels there sit in small patches
  (pasture, roadsides, conservation grassland, wetland edges) inside mixed cells, so a cover
  filter would drop most of the region's fires. Fire density still rises about five-fold from
  the least to the most herbaceous cells, and the seasonal shape is the same at every level of
  cover, so these are fires in herbaceous patches. Herbaceous wetland matters here: fire cells
  hold 5 % on average against 1.4 % for the region. The satellite green-up and curing dates of
  a typical cell in this region (52 % cropland) mostly describe crops.

**Burned area (MTBS).** MTBS maps 10,428 wildfires (types Wildfire and Wildland Fire Use) in
the lower 48 for 2001–2024; 96 % of them link to an FPA-FOD record, and for 96 % the MTBS
ignition date is within a day of the FPA-FOD discovery date. Prescribed fires (9,262) and the
type "Other" (2,069, mostly the Southeast, almost none in FPA-FOD) are left out. Large fires
(1,000 acres or more in FPA-FOD) are found in MTBS at a steady 71–91 % a year through 2023,
but only 62 % in 2024: MTBS has not finished mapping 2024. In the pilot regions MTBS wildfires
burned about 260,000 km² over the period, 62 % (monsoon Southwest) to 83 % (interior West) of it on
herbaceous fuel; the upper Midwest has few MTBS fires (about 190, 3,000 km²), so burned area
is a weak outcome there.

**Active fire (VIIRS).** NASA FIRMS 375 m detections for the lower 48, 2012–2025 (S-NPP) and
2018–2025 (NOAA-20). After removing static and industrial heat sources, volcanoes and offshore
detections (13–26 % of the raw record), each year holds 260,000–590,000 vegetation-fire
detections, 57,000–246,000 of them in the pilot regions (most in 2020 and 2021); 4–5 % are
low confidence. The two satellites agree within 5 % in the pilot regions in 2019–2023. S-NPP
has outage days in fire season (late July to August 2022, June–July 2024, a few in November
2024), which cost about a fifth of its 2024 detections relative to NOAA-20; NOAA-20 fills
those days.

**Linking satellite detections to reported fires.** Each detection is matched to an MTBS
perimeter (widened by 750 m) active at the time, or else to the nearest FPA-FOD fire within its
size-based search radius and burning dates; detections on cells that are half or more cropland
are flagged. In the western pilot regions 57–79 % of detections belong to reported wildfires,
almost all of them large MTBS fires; the rest are mostly prescribed burns, agricultural burning
(the Central Valley in California) and small fires. In the Great Plains only 32 % belong to
reported wildfires, and in the upper Midwest 3 %: two-thirds of its detections are on cropland
and nearly all the rest match no reported fire, which points to crop-residue and prescribed
prairie burning. Satellite fire growth is therefore not used as an outcome in the upper
Midwest, where fire counts and acres from FPA-FOD carry the analysis, and the satellite record
stops at 2024 because detections after that cannot yet be matched to reported fires.

**Burned area: FPA-FOD rather than MTBS.** MTBS maps only fires of 1,000 acres or more in the
West (500 in the East). In the western pilot regions those are 7–19 % of fires of 10 acres or
more but 87–95 % of burned area; in the upper Midwest they are 2.5 % of fires and 57 % of
burned area, and MTBS has not finished mapping 2024. FPA-FOD final sizes cover every fire of
10 acres or more through 2024.

**How the study handles them (decided October 17).** The main outcome counts fires of all
causes, which run continuously through the reporting change; lightning and human starts are
compared for 2001–2019 only (California: totals only), with a check that counts
unknown-cause fires as human, since their seasonal pattern matches human fires (r 0.90–1.00).
Lightning fire counts are no longer used as an ignition term. In the upper Midwest every fire
is kept, herbaceous wetland counts as herbaceous fuel, and the green-up and curing timing comes
from cells that are at least 35 % herbaceous (also in the Great Plains), applied to the whole
region; fires in the most herbaceous third of cells are a check. Burned area comes from
FPA-FOD final fire sizes (credited to the discovery week, so it is read by season and year, on
a log scale); MTBS perimeters are kept to link satellite detections to large fires and to
check what fuel those fires burned (2001–2023). S-NPP stays the single satellite series;
whole days with no S-NPP data are filled from NOAA-20 where it has data, the filled weeks are
flagged, and a check run leaves them out.

## Dryness baselines (built October 18)

Four dryness measures are computed from daily PRISM for every 4 km cell, 2001–2025, and
averaged by region and day (equally and weighted by herbaceous fuel share):

- **Rainfall minus potential evaporation over the last 60 days** (mm; Hargreaves potential
  evaporation from daily minimum and maximum temperature). This is the simple baseline: it
  reads directly as "how far rainfall has fallen behind evaporative demand", and the fire
  model is fitted with it first.
- **1000-hour dead fuel moisture** (%), the NFDRS 1978 model (Fosberg et al. 1981; Bradshaw et
  al. 1984; Cohen and Deeming 1985): a daily equilibrium moisture from day and night
  temperature and humidity, raised on rain days by rain duration, averaged over 7 days and
  moved part of the way toward that average each week. Most of its weight falls on the last
  two months of weather. PRISM has no humidity or rain duration, so humidity comes from the
  vapour pressure deficit and temperature (constant vapour pressure through the day), and rain
  duration from the daily amount with the NFDRS rule (0.25 inch per hour where April–September
  rainfall is below half the potential evaporation, 0.05 elsewhere, at most 8 hours). It replaces the simple baseline in a second fit; if it does
  not improve the held-out years, the simple one is reported.
- **Checks:** the Keetch–Byram drought index and the 30-day mean vapour pressure deficit.
- **Snow:** a degree-day snowpack (snow when the daily mean temperature is at or below 1 °C,
  melt of 3 mm per °C per day above 0 °C) gives the share of each region under snow and a
  yearly snow-off date, used in the Great Plains and upper Midwest.

To show what the 1000-hour value follows, its weekly departures from normal are compared
region by region with those of the 60-day water balance and the 30-day vapour pressure deficit.
The calculation was checked against an independent day-by-day implementation written from the
published equations (agreement within 0.0001 % moisture).

## Results (October 19, preliminary)

The test fits one model of weekly fire counts across the six pilot regions, with each region's
typical fire season, then adds a dryness measure, then the phenology measure: how much more (or
less) of the herbaceous fuel is cured that week than in a typical year. Each version predicts
every year after being fitted to the other years, and the gain in held-out prediction is the
answer.

- **Dryness matters everywhere**, for fire starts and for fire growth. The 1000-hour fuel moisture
  predicts better than the 60-day water balance overall (not in California), so its extra
  nonlinear detail carries information.
- **Phenology adds to fire growth.** Satellite fire growth (pixel-days, 2012–2024) is predicted
  better with phenology in about three years of four, in every region, and the gain holds over
  the 1000-hour baseline too.
- **Phenology adds little to the number of fire starts overall.** The gain is small and uncertain
  for all causes. It is clearer for human-caused fires (counting unknown causes as human) and
  absent for lightning fires, which fits the idea that people start fires in the cured-grass
  windows of spring and fall while lightning comes with the summer storms whatever the fuel.
- **Direction:** in every region, weeks with more cured fuel than usual have more fire.
- **Season:** in California the fire season opens the same week half the grass is typically
  cured; in the upper Midwest the spring fire window closes about four weeks after half the
  fuel has greened.

In California and the upper Midwest the fire curve follows the cured share closely; in the Southwest the fire season peaks in June as spring-active cells green and ends with the monsoon green-up; in the Great Plains the spring fires stop at green-up and the summer fires (mostly lightning) burn while the grass is green.", "Six small panels, one per pilot region, each with a blue fire-season curve and an orange typical-cured-share curve by week of the year.")

### Checks

Each check changes one thing and asks whether phenology still improves held-out predictions. The
blue line is the main result; a check that keeps its dot near the line passes.

```{r fig-fire-checks}
#| results: asis
show_fig("fire_checks", "Phenology's gain in held-out prediction, per year, pooled over the pilot regions, for the main result and each check (dot = estimate, line = 90 % bootstrap interval over years; for the shuffled years, the median and range of 20 shuffles). Gains are in held-out log score per year; fire growth is modelled on a log scale, so its scale differs from the fire-start panels. An extra term with no information scores about −0.5 per year for starts and −1.3 for growth (the shuffles), so that, not zero, is the bar to clear.", "Dot-and-interval chart with twelve rows (main result and eleven checks) and three columns (all fire starts, human and unknown starts, fire growth).")
```


- *Fires changing the satellite dates.* Leaving out every cell that burned that year or the year
  before (3–11 % of cells) leaves the gains unchanged, so the phenology signal is not made by the
  fires themselves.
- *Chance.* Giving each year's phenology to other years at random (20 times) makes predictions worse
  every time; the real phenology beats all 20 shuffles for both fire starts and fire growth.
- *Dates instead of shares.* A model using the year's green-up and curing dates (one number per
  region and year) does worse than the weekly share of fuel cured: what matters is how much of the
  fuel has cured, not a single regional date.
- *Forecast dates.* Curing dates predicted two weeks ahead from weather (the curing rules' method,
  refitted for every region and checked on years left out) are a little closer to the satellite
  dates than the typical date (1–3 days better, r 0.30–0.50), but they add nothing to fire
  prediction. The fire signal is in the observed fuel state, which the weather forecast does not
  capture.
- *Same-week weather.* Adding this week's vapour pressure deficit leaves most of the phenology
  gain (growth +41 instead of +46), so the cured share is not just a stand-in for a hot, dry week.
- *The GSI.* A cured share from NFDRS2016 GSI dates gains as much, but almost all of it in the
  monsoon Southwest, and much of it disappears once this week's VPD is in the model: the GSI's value
  for fire is mostly its VPD term. The satellite adds information the GSI lacks in California and
  the Great Plains; the GSI adds the Southwest's pre-monsoon dryness.
- *Real-time cured share.* Built only from the satellite composites available each week, the cured
  share runs about two weeks behind and does not carry the fire-growth signal, even when each
  week's curve is smoothed over the data available so far; a monitoring product would need data
  faster than 16-day composites.
- *Ground check.* At single NPN grass sites the satellite and ground curing departures agree only
  modestly (r 0.35); averaged over a region's sites in a year, the scale used here, they agree at r
  0.66 (Great Plains 0.74, monsoon Southwest 0.84, upper Midwest 0.20).
- *Satellite delay.* Using the cured share as the satellite showed it two weeks earlier keeps about
  half of the gain for fire growth and loses most of it for fire starts: the signal is in the
  current week's fuel state, so monitoring needs to be timely.
- *C3/C4 gap.* Two-peaked greenness curves are rare in the northern and central Great Plains (314
  of 47,900 cells) and common in the southern Plains (43 %), where the two peaks are spring and fall
  growth around a summer drought trough. Fires there are most frequent in that summer trough, so
  there is no fire dip between growth pulses; the 4 km satellite curves cannot separate the C3 and
  C4 pulses of northern mixed prairie. The [NPN curing study](npn_study.html) answered it from the
  ground (October 20): at sites with both grass types, warm-season (C4) grasses reach 50 % green in
  late spring, four to six months before the cool-season (C3) grasses cure, in every year and every
  region checked (Great Plains, southern Plains, upper Midwest, mid-South). The two pulses overlap;
  there is no C3-to-C4 gap on the ground, so a mid-season dip in fire could only come from weather.
- *Ground observations.* The NPN ground study found the same limit as the forecast test: weather
  explains little of the year-to-year change in when grasses cure at a site, so curing has to be
  observed, not forecast from weather.

- *All-cause fire starts are fragile.* Their pooled gain is +18 over 2001–2024 but +8 over
  2002–2024: one year carries half of it. The fire-growth and human-cause results do not hinge on
  single years like that.

These are first numbers from 13–24 seasons per region; they will change as the analysis is
reviewed.

## Decisions so far

| Date | Decision | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Oct 1 2026 | Fire activity as a regional, seasonal check on phenology, not fire by fire | Removes the scale mismatch between fires and point observations |
| Oct 17 2026 | A companion study with its own page; code shared with the regions work | Uses the regions, satellite dates and typical-date maps directly |
| Oct 17 2026 | PRISM as the only weather source; dead-fuel moisture computed from it | One weather source across the project keeps the methods simple |
| Oct 17 2026 | FPA-FOD 7th edition (1992–2024), MTBS, VIIRS S-NPP | Long record of starts; consistent single-sensor growth series |
| Oct 17 2026 | Main outcome: wildfires of 10 acres or more by week, by cause | Fuel condition decides whether a start grows; larger fires are reported consistently |
| Oct 17 2026 | Pilot regions 3, 6, 12, 11, 10 and 13 | Grass and shrub fire regimes in the West, plus the northern Plains and upper Midwest partners |
| Oct 17 2026 | Main outcome counts all causes; lightning vs human for 2001–2019 only; California totals only | Cause reporting changed in 2020–21 (unknown causes up to 50–86 % in California); total counts are unaffected |
| Oct 17 2026 | No lightning-count ignition term; a 2020-onward indicator as a check | Lightning counts were relabelled after 2019 and are partly the outcome |
| Oct 17 2026 | Upper Midwest: all fires kept; herbaceous wetland counted as fuel; phenology from cells at least 35 % herbaceous (also Great Plains) | Fires sit in small herbaceous patches inside cropland cells, whose satellite dates track crops |
| Oct 17 2026 | Burned area from FPA-FOD final sizes; MTBS for linking detections and the fuel-burned check (2001–2023) | MTBS covers only large fires and has not finished 2024; FPA-FOD covers all fires of 10 acres or more |
| Oct 17 2026 | S-NPP outage days filled from NOAA-20 (flagged; check run without them) | Outages fall in fire season; the satellites agree within 5 % otherwise |
| Oct 18 2026 | Satellite fire growth 2012–2024 only, and not in the upper Midwest | Detections after 2024 cannot be matched to reported fires; in the upper Midwest 97 % are agricultural or prescribed burning |
| Oct 18 2026 | Linking screen kept as is; Great Plains check run counting all non-cropland detections | In the western regions unmatched detections spread across the year (burning outside the fire season); in the Great Plains they share the summer peak |
| Oct 18 2026 | Weeks are fixed 7-day blocks from January 1 (last one or two days of the year in week 52) | Every year has the same 52 weeks on the same dates |
| Oct 19 2026 | Checks before the write-up: leave out cells burned that year or the year before; give each year's phenology to other years at random; test forecast curing dates (weather adjustment in every region); test green-up and curing dates directly; C3/C4 gap test in two-pulse prairie | The phenology gain must not come from fires changing the satellite dates, and must hold for dates a manager could know in advance |
| Oct 19 2026 | Same-week VPD check; GSI (NFDRS2016, FEMS with KBDI) cured share compared with the satellite's; NPN ground check at the regional scale | Rule out a hot spell driving both curing and fire; test the operational index; check the satellite against the ground |
| Oct 19 2026 | Real-time cured share from the composites available each week, raw and smoothed to date | A test of whether curing could be monitored in time to use |
| Oct 19 2026 | C3/C4 reported as a limitation of the satellite test; ground timing passed to the NPN study | The 4 km curves cannot separate the two pulses in northern mixed prairie |
| Oct 18 2026 | A 60-day rainfall-minus-evaporation baseline alongside the 1000-hour fuel moisture | The 1000-hour equations are nonlinear and need humidity and rain duration that PRISM lacks; the simple measure is readable and shows whether the operational index adds anything |

: Study decisions {.striped}
